title: 84 per cent consumers expect greater healthcare convenience: Bain survey
summary: The findings also highlight growing pressure on clinicians, with one in five doctors actively considering leaving their current employer, primarily due to excessive workload, lack of recognition and burnout.
contentHtml:
The findings also highlight growing pressure on clinicians, with one in five doctors actively considering leaving their current employer, primarily due to excessive workload, lack of recognition and burnout.

Asia-Pacific healthcare systems are facing growing pressure as rising patient expectations, an overstretched clinical workforce and increasing demand for coordinated care accelerate the need for new healthcare delivery models and AI-enabled support, according to Bain & Company’s 2026 Asia-Pacific Front Line of Healthcare Report. 

Based on surveys of 6,300 consumers across nine Asia-Pacific markets and 600 doctors in the region, the report highlights widening gaps between consumer expectations and healthcare experiences, clinician dissatisfaction and challenges in adopting AI at scale.

The report covers consumers across Australia, China, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam, as well as doctors in Australia and the Philippines.

The report finds that 84 per cent of consumers expect greater convenience from healthcare systems, while 71 per cent expect doctors to be more responsive through channels such as phone, WhatsApp and email. Three in five consumers now schedule regular checkups and screenings, compared with 47 per cent in 2023. 

Additionally, 57 per cent of consumers report receiving care in at least one alternative setting, including telehealth, urgent care clinics, walk-in clinics, home-based care and ambulatory surgery centres. 95 per cent want a single touchpoint to manage their healthcare, up from 70 per cent in 2019.

The findings also highlight growing pressure on clinicians, with one in five doctors actively considering leaving their current employer, primarily due to excessive workload, lack of recognition and burnout. Around one in three doctors report significant workplace inefficiencies, including excessive paperwork, repetitive tasks and delays caused by fragmented workflows and coordination gaps.

AI is emerging as an opportunity to address some of these challenges, with doctors identifying reduced administrative burden and workload as its most significant potential benefits. Nearly three in four consumers report feeling comfortable with at least one AI-enabled healthcare application.

However, approximately one in three doctors say their organisations are not prepared to deploy AI at scale, citing unclear strategies, limited training and insufficient clinician involvement as key barriers. The report also emphasises that in-person appointments remain the preferred channel for non-acute symptoms, with both consumers and doctors viewing telehealth as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, in-person care.

To address these challenges, Bain & Company identifies five strategic priorities for healthcare stakeholders: becoming a trusted coordination point for patients across settings and channels; redesigning care journeys around important patient experiences; implementing value-based care models focused on outcomes; embedding AI into core operating models and redesigning workflows; and strengthening clinician engagement by improving the workforce experience and equipping clinicians to lead transformation.
